cases.name: Caitlin Kelley Walsh Aldridge
cases.about:
Her obituary said, "She grew up on the West Side, attended St. Paul's Open School, graduated from Cretin-Derham Hall in 1998, and the University of Minnesota Morris in 2002.
She joined the West Side Boosters as one of the first girl players in 5th grade, playing guard and tackle. In 1994, she became the first girl to play football at Cretin-Derham Hall. Most of her clothes were Vikings gear. Over the last 20 years, she spent Fall Sunday and Monday nights cheering for her team with her closest friends and their growing squad.
Caitlin's dedication showed up in her professional life in her commitment to strengthening our community and eliminating oppression through out school time youth programs. She spent most of her career as a leader on the youth programs team at the YWCA of Minneapolis, where she built lasting friendships with her colleagues and young people.

Her kindness will live within each of us. Casey always knew the perfect gift, knew other people's important dates, and made people feel loved. She showed up when people needed her. There are few pictures of her alone as she cared most about documenting moments with the people she loved."
cases.narrative: He told police they were arguing and she laughed off an allegation he made, and he got so angry he shot her once in the back of the head with a gun he kept under the pillow. He then drove to the police headquarters and turned himself in.

cases.name: Corrina Woodhull
cases.about:
She was an active part of an area drug addiction recovery program whose participants describe her as an inspiration. Corinna's mother, Linda Castle, said her daughter was someone who loved to help people who would not or could not help themselves, including Castillo. Her family said they encouraged her not to marry him since he had eight prior felony convictions, including violent crimes.

"She thought she could save him," her mother said. "That her love would help them live a life together."
cases.narrative:
He allegedly pulled out a knife and stabbed her repeatedly to death in front of both of their family. He had reportedly whispered in her ear before stabbing her, and Woodhull reportedly “shook her head no” after Castillo had whispered in her ear, and that he had been holding her hand and kissed her before he attacked.

Two witnesses estimated Castillo stabbed Woodhull 20 times and another said it was about 10 times. An autopsy found she had a stab wound to her chest that penetrated her breast and heart, and additional sharp force injuries to her face, chest and upper extremities

cases.name: Carrie Marie Shobe Kwok
cases.about:
Kwok is being remembered by family and friends as gentle soul who was extremely generous.

'She helped tons of people. She always wanted to take care of others,' Kwok's sister Julie Shobe told KSTP. 'I thought I would die before her, so it's crazy. Terribly sad.' 

Shobe said Kwok was a member of the Lowertown Lofts Artist Cooperative in St. Paul, which became her main creative outlet.

'She had a lot of interests,' Shobe said. 'She made clothes out of vintage fabrics or she repurposed antiques. She made shirts out of old tablecloths, like women's wear.'

The co-op wrote a social media post immediately after the news of the shooting spread, before Kwok or the suspect was identified.

'This afternoon one of our members was shot and killed while working on an art project outside of our building. We don't have a lot of information right now, but we are working closely with the authorities to resolve this tragic event,' the co-op wrote on Facebook. 

The statement continued: 'We ask that our friends and neighbors not speculate about the situation. Our community is in shock and grief as we grapple with the unimaginable.'

Later, Kwok's friends at the co-op memorialized her, speaking to reporters just beside the mural she died while working on

Shobe said Kwok was a devout Christian, something that is a comfort to them

Later, Kwok's friends at the co-op memorialized her, speaking to reporters just beside the mural she died while working on.

'The curiosity that I mentioned earlier was there. She loved life,' said Ben Krywosz, the president of the co-op.

Tara Tieso described Kwok as 'sparkly.'

'Every time she talked to you, you saw little sparkly things around her,' Tieso said.

'As she passed, she was in a place that she loved so, so very much,' Tieso added, explaining that several other artists were at the scene with her. 'She knew that we loved her.'
cases.narrative: He allegedly shot her execution-style as she kneeled down and painted a mural in an alley.
